tldr: We present Adaptive-MHE, a sampling-based adaptive model predictive control framework for legged robots that estimates unknown object mass and floor friction online while manipulating objects. It requires neither dynamic differentiation nor contact sensors. Even when payload mass or floor slipperiness changes mid-task, real-world hardware experiments demonstrate tracking performance nearly matching a controller with access to ground-truth parameters.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed Adaptive-MHE framework. The upper-level moving horizon estimator (MHE) estimates physical parameters of the object and terrain from a recent measurement window at 1–2 Hz. The lower-level whole-body controller (MPOPI) uses these estimated parameters to generate control inputs in real time at 100 Hz.
overview:
Loco-manipulation—where a quadruped robot pushes and transports large objects while walking—is expected to find wide applications in delivery, disaster response, and beyond. However, in real environments, physical properties such as payload mass, center of mass, and floor friction coefficients are rarely known in advance. Conventional model predictive control (MPC) typically relies on fixed parameters. When a payload suddenly becomes heavier or the floor becomes slippery, the robot may fail to reach its goal due to insufficient push force, or slip and lose its balance.

To address this, the authors developed a framework for online physical parameter identification without any gradient computation. Because contact dynamics in legged robots are discontinuous and non-differentiable, they employ sampling-based system identification, running parallel simulations to find parameters that best match recorded observations. They extended this approach into moving horizon estimation (MHE), which uses only a recent window of data, and coupled it asynchronously with MPOPI, another sampling-based MPC algorithm.

The framework was validated across five simulation tasks (straight-line pushing, circular trajectory pushing, mid-task mass changes, terrain friction transitions, and single-leg kicking) as well as experiments on a Unitree Go1 quadruped robot. Even when the payload mass abruptly increased from 3 kg to 4 kg or the surface switched to artificial turf, the robot promptly re-estimated the parameters from its altered motion, increased its pushing force, and successfully transported the object to the goal position with accuracy nearly equal to a controller provided with ground-truth parameters.
contributions: Formulated a derivative-free, sampling-based moving horizon estimation (MHE) framework for online system identification that operates reliably even under discontinuous contact dynamics.
Unified sampling-based parameter estimation and sampling-based MPC (MPOPI) into a single cohesive framework, realizing the world's first sampling-based adaptive MPC for legged loco-manipulation.

Demonstrated on a physical quadruped robot that unknown mass variations and floor friction transitions can be identified and adapted to using only state histories of the robot and object, without relying on force or contact sensors.

sections.heading: Challenges in pushing unknown payloads across unknown environments
sections.summary: Humans and animals seamlessly use various parts of their bodies to transport objects in unfamiliar settings, yet tasks involving frequent, discontinuous contacts remain a major challenge for robots. A mechanism is needed that can directly infer parameters from interaction data and incorporate them into control, without relying on exact prior parameter tuning or differentiable simulators.
sections.details:
Humans and animals skillfully traverse rough terrain and manipulate objects far larger than themselves by flexibly utilizing different parts of their bodies. Replicating this behavior on legged robots, however, remains exceptionally difficult.

The primary hurdle is that physical parameters—such as object mass and ground friction—are not known beforehand. When these values deviate, fixed-parameter controllers often slip or fail to generate adequate pushing force, leading to task failure. Reinforcement learning methods with domain randomization can help, but they cannot handle parameters outside the distribution specified during training.

Furthermore, classical system identification (Sys-ID) techniques often assume differentiable dynamics (gradients), making them difficult to apply directly to loco-manipulation where feet, ground, and payloads make and break contact abruptly.

To tackle this challenge, this work proposes a moving horizon estimation (MHE) scheme that estimates parameters via sampling over a recent observation window without using gradients. By coupling this estimation module with a sampling-based MPC, the authors established the first unified sampling-based adaptive control framework capable of handling non-differentiable contact dynamics.

sections.heading: Where reinforcement learning, classical control, and sampling approaches stand today
sections.summary: While reinforcement learning and model-based control are leading paradigms for quadruped loco-manipulation, both struggle with online adaptation to unknown environments. This work aims to close the loop online by leveraging recent advancements in sampling-based system identification and sampling-based MPC.
sections.details:
### II-A Loco-Manipulation for quadruped Robots
Reinforcement learning (RL) for whole-body control has demonstrated strong generalization, but policies are typically trained within a fixed distribution defined by domain randomization. Adapting to out-of-distribution environments requires retraining or additional fine-tuning. On the other hand, model-based optimal control incurs prohibitive computational cost in contact-rich settings, making real-time parameter estimation within the control loop extremely difficult.

Recently, GPU-accelerated sampling-based MPC (such as MPPI) has attracted substantial interest for its ability to handle discontinuous and non-convex dynamics through massively parallel rollouts. Even so, existing frameworks have generally assumed that environmental parameters are known in advance.

### II-B System Identification and Parameter Adaptation
Many robot system identification (Sys-ID) methods require differentiable dynamics or explicit contact detection, rendering them ill-suited for tasks with frequent contact mode transitions. While the recently proposed SPI (Sampling-based Parameter Identification) bypassed differentiability constraints using parallel sampling, it was strictly an offline method and could not track dynamic environmental changes occurring during execution.

Adaptive-MHE sets itself apart by advancing the benefits of sampling-based identification into an online moving horizon estimator and coupling it in real time with sampling-based MPC.

sections.heading: Two core building blocks: MPOPI and SPI
sections.summary: The proposed framework builds upon two foundations: MPOPI, a sampling-based whole-body MPC, and SPI, a sampling-based parameter identification method. The former explores control actions while the latter explores parameters, both solving their problems without derivatives via evolutionary strategies and parallel rollouts.
sections.details:
### III-A MPOPI (Model Predictive Path Integral with CMA-ES)
MPOPI enhances MPPI, a prominent sampling-based MPC algorithm, by combining it with the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES). Unlike vanilla MPPI or CMA-ES alone, MPOPI iteratively updates both the mean and covariance over multiple inner loops ($L$ loops), systematically improving sample quality. This significantly boosts search efficiency, allowing the controller to discover optimal joint command sequences with fewer rollout samples.

### III-B SPI (Sampling-based Parameter Identification)
SPI identifies physical parameters $\theta$—such as robot mass, inertia, and actuator characteristics—via zero-order optimization without computing gradients. Trajectory data collected from hardware is sliced into short clips, and candidate parameters are evaluated via parallel rollouts in simulation. CMA-ES is employed to update the distribution of parameter candidates so as to minimize the squared error between recorded and simulated trajectories. However, SPI was designed as an offline method using an entire pre-collected dataset, making it unusable for online adaptation during loco-manipulation.

sections.heading: Running estimation and control concurrently: How Adaptive-MHE works
sections.summary: The proposed approach runs two modules asynchronously: MHE, which estimates parameters from recent interaction data, and MPOPI, which handles whole-body control. Because both rely on sampling-based search over the same dynamical model, neither gradient computations nor explicit contact mode switching detection are required.
sections.details:
### IV-A Moving Horizon Estimator
The proposed MHE maintains a sliding window of recent trajectory data from the robot and the manipulated object (base pose, velocities, joint positions, and joint velocities). Rather than processing the entire history, it extracts the latest window at each update interval $\Delta t_{\mathrm{update}}$ to re-estimate parameters. Moreover, it runs asynchronously on a separate CPU thread at 1–2 Hz, completely avoiding interference with the real-time control loop.

### IV-B Whole-body Controller (MPOPI)
MPOPI operates at 100 Hz. Standard MPOPI performs $L_{\mathrm{MPOPI}}$ distribution update loops every cycle, which incurs substantial computational overhead. To mitigate this, the authors exploit the periodicity of legged locomotion: multi-loop distribution updates are executed only when contact modes switch (between stance and swing phases), whereas other control cycles warm-start from the previous distribution. This strategy significantly curtails computational cost without sacrificing search capability.

### IV-C Adaptive-MHE Formulation
The estimator and controller share a common parameterized dynamics model $f(p)$. The MHE objective is formulated as a nonlinear least-squares problem that penalizes discrepancies between predicted and observed states, augmented by a regularization term (weights on mass, inertia, and friction) relative to the prior estimate $\hat{p}_t^-$.

To solve this, $B$ parameter candidates are sampled from a Gaussian distribution centered at the prior estimate, and each is rolled out across the data window. Samples with lower costs are aggregated via log-ranked weighted averaging, and the distribution mean is updated with learning rate $\alpha$. The resulting updated estimate $\hat{p}_t$ is passed to the controller, immediately updating the internal model used for planning.

sections.heading: Validation results in simulation and hardware experiments
sections.summary: Using a Unitree Go1, five simulation tasks involving sudden mass changes and abrupt floor friction transitions were evaluated alongside physical hardware experiments. The framework showed dramatic performance gains over fixed-parameter baselines, performing on par with a controller that has access to ground-truth values.
sections.details:
### V-A Task Definitions and setups
Evaluations were conducted on a Unitree Go1 with a target velocity of 0.2 m/s across five tasks (T1–T5):
- **T1: Single Goal Pushing** (pushing an unknown object along a straight path)
- **T2: Circular Pushing** (continuously pushing along a curved trajectory with changing directions)
- **T3: Mass Adaptation** (box mass changes abruptly mid-transport)
- **T4: Terrain Friction Adaptation** (crossing a boundary from friction coefficient $\mu=0.4$ to $\mu=0.8$)
- **T5: Single-leg Manipulation** (pushing a box sideways using a single front leg while the robot body remains stationary)

Three methods were compared: "True" (controller provided with ground-truth parameters from the start), "Baseline" (fixed parameters from offline identification, corresponding to SPI), and the proposed "Adaptive-MHE".

### V-B Ablation and Simulation Study
A sensitivity analysis was conducted across seven hyperparameters over 15 random seeds, including update iterations $L_{\mathrm{MHE}}$, sample size $B$, update interval $\Delta t_{\mathrm{update}}$, horizon length $H$, learning rate $\alpha$, and regularization weights. Results indicated that an overly high learning rate or an excessively long horizon degraded success rates, allowing the authors to establish optimal default parameters for hardware deployment.

In the Task T4 comparison (TABLE I), while the Baseline showed an extremely low success rate, Adaptive-MHE drastically reduced goal-reaching errors and control effort, matching the performance of the True controller. Furthermore, across all tasks in TABLE II, Adaptive-MHE achieved significantly lower root mean square errors (RMSE) in velocity and path tracking compared to the Baseline.

### V-C Real-world demonstration
In physical robot experiments, the robot initially pushed a 3 kg basket, after which a 1 kg weight was manually added mid-motion (total 4 kg). The Baseline stalled before reaching the target due to insufficient push force, whereas Adaptive-MHE promptly re-estimated the mass from the altered robot dynamics, increased pushing effort, and reached the goal marker.

Similarly, when pushing a box from a concrete floor onto a high-friction artificial grass mat, the Baseline became stuck immediately upon entering the mat. In contrast, Adaptive-MHE detected the elevated resistance, increased pushing force in real time, and completed the transfer.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: By integrating sampling-based MHE with sampling-based MPC, the authors established an adaptive control framework that operates without dynamic gradients or handcrafted adaptation heuristics. High robustness demonstrated in both simulation and hardware marks an encouraging step toward autonomous operation in unstructured environments.
sections.details:
This paper presented Adaptive-MHE, a framework that couples sampling-based moving horizon estimation for online system identification with sampling-based MPC.

It offers a contact-resilient adaptive control framework for legged systems that does not require differentiable dynamics or manual tuning of empirical adaptation laws. Simulation and hardware experiments demonstrated that even under abrupt mid-task variations in object mass or terrain friction, the framework achieves trajectory and velocity tracking comparable to controllers given ground-truth parameters, dramatically reducing terminal goal errors relative to fixed-parameter baselines.

sections.heading: [Appendix] Detailed behavioral analysis across tasks
sections.summary: The appendix provides an in-depth analysis of velocity tracking and parameter convergence curves across the benchmark tasks. It highlights that the proposed framework is effective not only for whole-body pushing, but also for intricate contact tasks where a single leg acts as a manipulator.
sections.details:
### Detailed Analysis of T1 and T2
In T1 (single-goal pushing), parameter mismatches directly manifested as a degradation in forward velocity tracking (target 0.2 m/s). In T2 (circular pushing), the Baseline drifted outward from the intended curve as the pushing direction changed. In contrast, Adaptive-MHE maintained a smooth circular path nearly identical to True, with cost distributions tightly peaked near zero.

### Parameter Tracking in T3 and T4
In T3 (where mass abruptly changed from 4 kg to 6 kg at $t = 10\text{ s}$), the estimated mass in Adaptive-MHE quickly converged to the true value shortly after the transition, keeping the velocity tracking RMSE remarkably low compared to the Baseline's 0.117 m/s. In T4 (terrain friction change), the friction estimate similarly converged to the ground truth within seconds of crossing the boundary.

### Detailed Analysis of T5 (Single-leg Manipulation)
In T5, where the robot pushes a box sideways by 0.5 m using only one front leg while maintaining a stationary torso, the final box positioning error was 0.42 m for Baseline, whereas Adaptive-MHE reduced it to 0.28 m, closely approaching the 0.12 m achieved by True. This confirms that online parameter adaptation provides significant performance gains even in delicate motions where a leg acts as an impromptu manipulator.

captions.F7: Forward velocity tracking results in task T2 (circular pushing). The proposed Adaptive-MHE (middle) maintains tracking fidelity (RMSE = 0.104 m/s) comparable to True (top), whereas Baseline (bottom) falls substantially below the 0.2 m/s reference due to parameter mismatch.
captions.F11: Final configurations of the robot and box after completing task T5 (single-leg manipulation). Compared to the fixed-parameter Baseline (c: error 0.42 m), Adaptive-MHE (b: error 0.28 m) pushes the box much closer to the target position achieved by True using ground-truth parameters (a: error 0.12 m).

takeaways: Even for contact-rich, non-differentiable tasks, parallel rollout-based sampling MHE enables online parameter identification at 1–2 Hz on a standard CPU thread.
Limiting MPC distribution updates to contact-mode transition points and leveraging warm-starting drastically reduces computational cost while preserving search capabilities.

Without expensive force or tactile sensors, sudden variations in mass and surface friction can be reliably estimated and compensated for purely through the position and velocity histories of the robot and object.
limitations: Assumes external observability of state variables (accurate positions, orientations, and velocities of both the robot and box), relying on environments such as motion capture.

In terrain friction adaptation, while the estimated friction coefficient converged to the true value, the improvement in closed-loop velocity tracking error was not as pronounced as it was during mass adaptation.
Because the estimator runs at 1–2 Hz on a CPU, a transient response time of a few seconds is incurred before adaptation is fully realized following an abrupt parameter change.
